## TL;DR

Task #1185 addresses an installed-upgrade restart notice that misclassified a systemd user service as hand-run when the process title was renamed. The current branch detects Linux service ownership from `/proc/<pid>/cgroup` and, when that is unavailable, checks whether the parent is systemd. It presents a restart-in-progress label and preserves the error reporting path. The QA record says plainly that a real hand-run or supervised restart was not performed in this session. I also fixed the reported changed-path test failures by making the Tailscale discovery tests independent of the host’s actual tailnet HTTP listener. The focused test file passes.

## Work and rationale

I resumed from the existing clean branch, read the task specification, and inspected the current supervisor detector, restart route, release notification, and the failing test file. The detector already used `systemctl status <pid>` as its first signal. On failure it now reads the process cgroup, extracts a `.service` unit, distinguishes the system user slice from a system unit, and classifies RepoOS-installed unit labels as managed. If cgroup inspection does not identify a unit, it checks the parent command; a systemd parent without a safely extracted unit remains uncertain instead of being treated as hand-run. On macOS the detector already maps launchd pids from launchctl output, and the existing test suite covers managed, external and hand-run outcomes.

The restart endpoint delegates to the verified restart helper and returns an explicit failure result when it cannot spawn the helper or when supervisor classification is uncertain. In the release notice, restart requests display “Restarting…” while accepted, and the client’s existing health reconnection path handles the replacement server. Errors are rendered in the notice. I retained the QA statement that no live restart was attempted: this environment did not control a real hand-run process or a systemd/launchd service, so an automated test cannot stand in for that operator check.

The handoff message identified four failures in `servers-command.test.ts`. Running the file reproduced them: their default HTTP discovery reached actual Bee RepoOS servers before consulting the injected mock SSH command, so results depended on live machine state. I updated the affected test calls to inject `httpDiscovery: async () => null` and set `annotateUrls: false`. These cases are testing SSH discovery/fallback behavior, so disabling the separate HTTP discovery and URL enrichment paths keeps the test focused and deterministic. The focused test run then passed all 15 cases.

## Approaches tried

I first reran `bun run test -- src/ui-app/tests/servers-command.test.ts` to confirm the queued failure. The assertion diffs showed real server rows from Bee, which established that the test was using the default network path rather than its mocked remote command. I then used the existing `httpDiscovery` seam to force the intended SSH fallback and disabled URL annotation, which otherwise triggers unrelated serve-status reads. I reran the focused file and confirmed the failures were resolved.

I ran `bun run fmt` after editing. Formatting completed successfully. The required changed-path RepoOS check remains the final verification step for this handoff.

## Challenges and blockers

This session cannot verify the product behavior against a live hand-run server, systemd user unit, or launchd job. The reported failure occurred on Bee, but no access to that host or its service manager is part of this run. The QA note therefore explicitly records “not performed” for the real restart and leaves that evidence for an operator. No test evidence or device result is inferred from the unit tests.

## Key learnings

The Tailscale collection tests had injected the SSH command but left HTTP peer discovery on its real default. That allowed a developer machine’s configured tailnet to alter unit-test outcomes. When a function has multiple I/O channels, a mock for only one channel does not fully isolate the test. Here the HTTP discovery seam and URL annotation option provide the appropriate boundaries. For restart detection, renamed process titles should not be treated as evidence of a hand-run process; operating-system ownership data such as a service cgroup or verifiable parent must drive the classification, with uncertainty retained when ownership cannot be proved.
